passages.t: Sing, barren woman: your Maker is your husband
passages.happening:
“Shout for joy, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth in song and cry aloud, you who have never travailed” (verse 1). The desolate woman will have more children than the one who has a husband (verse 1).

‘Enlarge the site of your tent, stretch out the curtains of your dwellings, do not hold back’ (verse 2). She is to lengthen the ropes and drive the stakes deep, because her descendants will spread to right and left and live in the empty cities (verse 3).

She is not to be afraid. She will forget the shame of her youth and the reproach of her widowhood (verse 4). ‘For your husband is your Maker’ (verse 5). The LORD has called her back like a wife deserted and wounded in spirit (verse 6).

‘For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back’ (verse 7). ‘In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 53 ended with the Servant seeing his offspring after bearing the sin of many. Chapter 54 shows what that looks like: a desolate woman suddenly surrounded by children.

For the exiles and for those who came back to an emptied Judah, a barren, widowed woman described their situation exactly. Jerusalem had been emptied by death and deportation after 587 or 586 BC, and the first groups who returned after Cyrus's decree were small. In that world a woman's security rested on her husband and her children. Barrenness was a deep grief and often a social shame, as with Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, and a widow with no sons had no one to protect her. The poem names every part of that: barren, deserted, widowed, rejected. Then it reverses each one.

The tent recalls Israel's ancestors. A family that grew added curtains, lengthened the ropes and drove the stakes deeper.

The marriage picture also answers the question of 50:1, whether God had divorced his people. He calls her back. The word for husband in verse 5 shares its letters with the name of Baal, the god Israel so often ran after. Zion's true husband is her Maker.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 1 of the church born by promise: “Rejoice, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth and cry aloud, you who have never travailed” (Galatians 4:27). Sarah's story stands behind the picture: ‘Sarai was barren; she had no children’ (Genesis 11:30).
passages.hard:
God says he forsook Zion for a brief moment (verse 7). Did God really forsake his people? And what does this poem say to someone who longs for a child?

Verses 7 and 8 say it plainly, and the text does not soften it. The exile was experienced as real abandonment, and Scripture lets God own it instead of blaming Babylon or chance. Some interpreters stress that the language is covenantal: God withdrew his protective presence, as Deuteronomy 31:17 had warned. Others stress the proportion the poem insists on: a brief moment against everlasting compassion. On any reading, the forsaking is temporary and the compassion is permanent.

The barren woman here is a city, Zion, and the children are her returning people. The poem uses the grief of childlessness because its hearers knew that grief well. It is not a promise of a child to any one person, and it gives no one a reason to see childlessness as a sign of God's displeasure. The Bible names Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, all childless for years, and blames none of them.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Zion is told to enlarge her tent before the children arrive. Ask what it would look like to make room for what God has promised but you cannot yet see. And ask whether you believe God's anger lasts a moment and his compassion for good.

passages.t: An oath like Noah's, and a city of jewels
passages.happening:
‘For to Me this is like the days of Noah, when I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth’ (verse 9). So God has sworn not to be angry with Zion again.

‘Though the mountains may be removed and the hills may be shaken, My loving devotion will not depart from you, and My covenant of peace will not be broken’ (verse 10).

God speaks to the afflicted city, ‘lashed by storms, without solace’ (verse 11). He will set her stones in antimony and lay her foundations with sapphires, make her pinnacles of rubies and her walls of precious stones (verses 11 and 12). ‘Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their prosperity’ (verse 13).

She will be established in righteousness, far from oppression and terror (verse 14). Whoever attacks her does so without God's sending, and will fall (verse 15). God made the smith who forges weapons (verse 16). ‘No weapon formed against you shall prosper’ (verse 17). This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The oath to Noah reaches back to the covenant after the flood, the oldest promise in Scripture that God will hold back his judgment. As he swore then, he swears now.

The word for loving devotion is chesed, love that keeps faith with a promise even when the other side has failed.

The jeweled city uses building language. Antimony was a dark mineral used as eye paint, as Jezebel painted her eyes with it. Here it becomes the mortar for gemstones, a picture of lavish, almost playful beauty. The identity of some of the stones is uncertain, as with many ancient gem names.

Verse 13 uses the word for one who is taught, the same word that described the Servant in 50:4, who was taught morning by morning. What the Servant was, his children become.

Verse 17 is the first place since chapter 40 where the word servants is plural. From here to the end of the book, God's faithful people are called his servants, the ones who inherit what the Servant won.
passages.later: God swore to Noah, ‘Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood’ (Genesis 9:11). Jesus quotes verse 13, ‘And they will all be taught by God’, and adds that everyone who has heard the Father comes to him (John 6:45). Revelation pictures the new Jerusalem with foundations of precious stones (Revelation 21:19).
passages.asks: God says his loving devotion will stay even if the mountains move. Ask what in your life feels as fixed as a mountain, and whether you trust God's love more than that. And ask what it would mean for you to be taught by the LORD, as the Servant was.
